scenario.user_message: Explain speculative decoding and when it stops helping.
scenario.notes: Gains depend on acceptance rate; a poor draft model is a net loss.

results.response:
Speculative decoding speeds up generation by letting a smaller "draft" model propose multiple tokens ahead, which a larger "target" model then verifies in a single batched forward pass. Instead of running the heavy target model once per token, you run it once per block of drafted tokens.

Crucially, this isn't an approximation; the method uses a modified rejection-sampling rule to ensure the final output follows the exact same probability distribution as if the target model had generated everything itself. This guarantees no quality loss, only throughput gains (Leviathan et al., ICML 2023).

It stops helping when the overhead outweighs the savings. Since every additional token in the draft requires *all* previous tokens to be accepted, the number of successfully generated tokens grows sublinearly, while the computational cost of the draft grows linearly. Eventually, the time spent generating the draft exceeds the time saved by verifying it, meaning the optimal draft length is often quite small.

Think about how the acceptance rate changes as you increase the draft size—what happens to the speedup ratio?

Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) encode position by rotating query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their absolute position [Su et al., RoFormer (2021)]. Because the attention score is calculated from the product of a query and a key, these absolute rotations cancel out during the dot product, leaving only the difference in position [Su et al., RoFormer (2021)].

This results in a relative encoding implemented through absolute rotations, meaning the model learns relationships based on distance rather than memorizing specific indices. Since there are no learned position parameters or additive bias terms, the logic holds regardless of how long the sequence becomes, allowing it to generalize beyond the training context length. Additionally, this structure means offsets cancel out naturally, so packing multiple documents together doesn't break the positional logic [Su et al., RoFormer (2021)].
